1:
Barnes marks this chapter as the parting of the ways. Up to here, he says, there may be diversities about words but no material difference about the writer’s meaning; from this point begins the divergence toward theories various, discordant, and many of them wild and fantastic. He states why: the scene now opens into the future, there is no designation of places, no designation of time that is necessarily unambiguous, and nothing in the symbols making it certain they could apply to only one class of events. Robertson draws the practical conclusion and refuses the enterprise: he will make no effort to refer the seals to persons or events past, present or future, but only to relate the symbolism to the other symbols of the book.

Two of them nevertheless place it. Clarke reports the supposition that from here to the eleventh chapter the calamities falling on the enemies of Christianity, and particularly the Jews, are set out under various images; Gill denies exactly that, since Jerusalem’s destruction had been accomplished some years before the vision, so that a vision of it would have been needless, and takes the first six seals of the pagan empire and the steps to its ruin. Clarke adds a point neither disputes, that the opening of a seal is not merely a declaration of what God will do but the exhibition of a purpose then accomplished, since whenever a seal is opened the sentence appears executed.

Ellicott stops on two words. The clause and see is doubtful, the manuscript authority for keeping and dropping it being about equally divided, so he is guided by context and asks whom the summons addresses. Not the seer, who was near already and had no occasion to draw nearer; not Christ, since it is hard to believe the living creature would so cry to the Lamb opening the scroll. He answers by asking who did come, and there is one answer — the horseman. From that he draws the sense: the living beings stand for animated nature, which groans and travails waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God, and they summon war and pestilence because through these lies the way for the coming of God’s Christ, so that their cry has an undertone sighing for the advent of the Prince of Peace.

The white horse is read as the gospel by three, for different reasons. Victorinus makes it the word of preaching sent into the world with the Holy Spirit, whose words the preachers sent forth as arrows reaching the human heart to overcome unbelief, and takes the crown as promised to those preachers. Bede has the Lord presiding over a Church made whiter than snow by grace and bearing the arms of spiritual teaching. Henry notices what a soldier would: white horses are generally refused in war because they make the rider a mark, but this Rider was sure of victory; and when Christ went to war one would think a helmet more proper than a crown, though the crown is given as the earnest of victory.

Bede alone reads the chapter as an outline. He notes that the seals are loosed first and the book then opened, the accustomed order purposely changed, and lays out the seven: in the first the glory of the primitive Church, in the following three the threefold war against it, in the fifth the glory of those who triumph, in the sixth the things to come in the time of Antichrist with a brief recapitulation, in the seventh the beginning of eternal rest. Robertson notes that the phrase for the Lamb’s opening recurs in rhythmical order at every seal until the last, where the particle changes to call attention to it; and Wesley says only that the first living creature is the one that looks eastward.
2:
Barnes asks a question none of the others ask: what exactly did the seer see? Was it a series of pictures drawn on successive portions of the volume as the seals broke, or a written description read aloud, or was the opening merely the occasion of a scenic representation? Nothing decides it, but he argues for the pictorial view on three grounds — that it was something in or on the volume, since he was invited to draw nearer; that each thing under the first five seals is capable of being painted; that the language is not what a man would use of a description merely read.

Who the first rider is divides them entirely. Clarke and Gill take him for the gospel: Clarke makes the bow the preaching that darts conviction into sinners’ hearts and the crown the kingdom’s emblem, Gill makes the white horse the apostolic ministry and matches the first two seals to Ephesus and Smyrna. Robertson notes that white is the colour of victory and of the Roman triumph, and admits it is tempting to identify this rider with the one on the white horse in chapter 19. Wesley refuses all of it and names a man: Nerva succeeded Domitian in the very year the Revelation was written, reigned scarcely a year alone and named Trajan; Trajan’s accession is the dawning of the seals, and in the year 108 he carried the bounds of the empire further than ever — we find no emperor like him for making conquests, since he aimed at nothing else and lived only to conquer.

Ellicott takes a third way, making the vision a portrait of its first readers. All agree the rider means victory; but a merely transient conqueror will not answer the words that he might conquer, and no picture of Roman world-victory would have conveyed the assured happiness the vision was designed to give. He therefore reads it as the reflex of early Christian hope — their hopes saw Christ ascended yet going forth in spiritual power — and adds: they were right in their faith and wrong in their expectation, right that he went forth conquering and would conquer, wrong in supposing the visions of war, famine and death would not intervene.

The red horse is agreed to mean war, and the disagreement is over whose. Clarke lists four candidates for the rider — Christ, Vespasian, the Roman armies, a Parthian king — and takes the taking of peace as the depriving of Judaea of tranquillity, fulfilled when the Jews killed one another during the Roman siege. Henry deliberately generalises against that: though some understand these seals of persecutions and others of the destruction of the Jews, they rather represent God’s terrible judgments at large upon those who make light of the covenant; and draws the moral that those who will not submit to the bow of the gospel must expect the sword of divine justice. Wesley dates it again: a temple to Peace had been dedicated in the year 75, but when Trajan ascended, peace was taken from the earth, and the war with the king of Dacia lasted five years and consumed abundance of men on both sides.

Wesley alone supplies a key to the four summonses: at each seal it was necessary to turn toward the quarter of the world it more immediately concerned, the first living creature looking east and the second west. Barnes explicitly denies any such significance, holding that there is no reason why the second creature rather than another should speak at the second seal, and that all that is designed is to show God’s providential government in each. Robertson keeps to the words: he notes the red is flame-coloured, that the sword here is the long battle sword, not the knife at the girdle, and observes, of men slaying one another, that this is what war does to perfection.
5:
Barnes works the black horse the way he worked the red, from the emblem outward. Black is in Scripture the image of fear, of famine, of death — our skin was black like an oven because of the terrible famine — and the Latin poets use it the same way. But he refuses to let the colour decide by itself: we should naturally look for some dire calamity, though which is not designated by the word black, and famine, pestilence, oppression, taxation, tyranny or invasion would all answer. What the calamity is must be determined by what follows in the symbol.

The balances narrow it, but not far. The word is properly a yoke, and so the beam of a pair of scales: something is to be weighed, to ascertain its quantity or value. Scales are ordinarily the emblem of justice, and if they stood alone we should look for a time of the exact administration of law; but they are also the emblem of exaction, as where the balance of deceit is in his hands, and joined with the sale of corn by weight they mean scarcity. Barnes therefore leaves it open between dearth and severe taxation and lets the proclamation settle it. Robertson keeps it simpler: the rider, like the spectral figure of hunger, carries a pair of scales, and this too is one of the fruits of war.

The proclamation is priced, and those who work the arithmetic agree. Clarke takes the measure as holding about what one man could consume in a day, and the penny as the denarius, the ordinary pay of a labourer: so each might obtain a bare subsistence by his daily labour, but could not provide for a family. Barley stands at three to one because it was the poorer aliment, given to Roman soldiers instead of wheat by way of punishment; and hurt not the oil and the wine means use them not as delicacies but for necessity. Robertson reads the clause as a ceiling rather than a threat — the proclamation forbids famine prices, and the prohibition is addressed to the nameless rider who represents Dearth.

Gill contributes one sentence, and it cuts against the historical reading. The voice from the midst of the living creatures is not, he says, the voice of Agabus to Paul — the very famine under Claudius that Clarke offers as the fulfilment — but of Christ, who was in the midst of them; and the Ethiopic version adds, as the voice of an eagle. Robertson hears it as the protest of nature against the horrors of famine, and observes that the vague as it were a voice is characteristic of this writer’s style.

Wesley calls it black famine, as the ancient poets term it, and turns the scales into doctrine: in plenty men scarce think it worth while to weigh everything, but in scarcity they are obliged to deliver by measure and weight; and the scales are also a token that all the fruits of the earth, and consequently the whole heavens with their courses, and all the seasons with whatsoever they produce in nature or in states, are subject to Christ, whose hand is wonderful not only in wars and victories but in the whole course of nature. He dates it as before, to Trajan’s reign in Egypt, which lies southward from Patmos and was the granary of the empire: an uncommon dearth at the very beginning of his reign obliged him to supply Egypt itself with corn from other countries, and in his thirteenth year the harvest failed for want of the rising of the Nile. That southward is his key to the third living creature; Clarke identifies it instead as the one with the face of a man; and Barnes says only that it is not apparent why this creature should take a particular interest here, nor necessary to show why.
7:
On the colour they converge. Barnes takes the word for yellowish-green, and says paleness is the most striking effect of death: red would denote the ravages of war, black those of sudden calamity, the pale famine or wasting disease. Robertson traces it to the word for tender green grass — we speak of a sorrel horse, never of a green horse — then notes that Homer used it of a face blanched by fear, so that the pale horse is a symbol of death and terror. Clarke produces the tag: pale death, a very usual poetic epithet, here beyond doubt since the text names the rider.

Barnes notices what is missing. No description is given of the rider’s aspect, and he bears no emblem — no sword, no spear, no bow. There is evident scope for the fancy to picture the form of the Destroyer, and just that kind of obscurity which contributes to sublimity — which is why this seal has furnished occasion for some of the greatest triumphs of the pencil. Robertson notes the broken grammar by which the name is attached, and calls Hades Death’s inseparable comrade.

Hades divides them a little. Barnes insists the word means the abode of the dead, where they dwell, not in the restricted modern sense of a place of punishment; the dead would be so numerous it would seem as if the pale nations of the dead had come again upon the earth. Clarke makes it the grave receiving the slain, and calls the figure a very elegant personification. Robertson gives the etymology — the unseen — recalls that Christ holds its keys, and refuses to settle the staging: it kept step with Death, on the same horse or another or on foot, John does not say. Wesley alone draws a structural conclusion: the four first seals concern living men, so death is properly introduced here and its companion only occasionally, and the fourth seal thus reaches to the borders of things invisible, comprised in the three last.

On the commission, Barnes limits the earth to the Roman world, declines to press the fourth part as exact, and distributes the instruments: the sword is war, hunger the famine that follows armies trampling the crops and shutting men in besieged cities, and death must mean what the other two do not, namely pestilence — the Hebrew word for pestilence being rendered by this same Greek word some fifty times in the Old Testament. Robertson says it more briefly: the four scourges of Ezekiel are reproduced here. Gill, who has read the earlier seals as the church’s history, changes tack: the pale might be the church, but not pale with persecution, for through that it was red — rather it is the sickly and dying state of the pagan Roman empire.

Wesley reads the seal as a climax. What came single and in a lower degree before comes now together and much more severely: the first seal brought victory, the second a great sword, the third a moderate dearth; here are famine and plague and wild beasts beside; and cites Aurelius Victor, that then the Tiber overflowed much more fatally than under Nerva, with a great destruction of houses, and there was a dreadful earthquake through many provinces, a terrible plague and famine, and many places consumed by fire. Then the causal chain, his real contribution: war brings on scarcity, and scarcity pestilence through want of wholesome sustenance, and pestilence, by depopulating the country, leaves the few survivors an easier prey to the wild beasts — thus these judgments make way for one another in the order here represented. He assigns the fourth living creature to the north; Barnes, consistent to the end, says no particular reason appears why the fourth should make this proclamation rather than another, and that it was merely poetic and appropriate to represent each in his turn.
9:
The staging changes and everyone notices: no living creature summons the seer at this seal. Barnes says no reason is given and none can be assigned, unless that having shown each of the four in turn there was no propriety in showing them again. Henry offers two guesses: the decorum of the vision, each creature having discharged its duty of monitor; or that this seal contains no new prophecy but opens a spring of support and consolation to those under tribulation. Clarke says it shorter: no new event is predicted, the whole intended to comfort the followers of God under persecution.

Where the altar stands is the sharpest disagreement here. Clarke states it flatly: the altar is upon earth, not in heaven. Barnes takes it for the altar of burnt sacrifice that stood before the temple, then observes that temple and altar were both destroyed before this book was written, so that this is vision, and the scene is undoubtedly laid in heaven. Robertson agrees on which altar and says why they are under it: the blood of the sacrifices was poured at the bottom of the altar. Wesley names both altars in the book, the golden altar of incense and the altar of burnt-offerings, and puts the martyrs at the foot of the latter. Henry alone puts them at the altar of incense, in the most holy place, in heaven at the foot of Christ.

The word souls splits them differently. Barnes takes it for one of the incidental proofs in the Bible that the soul does not cease to exist at death, nor sleep till the resurrection: these are shown remembering what occurred on earth and engaged in prayer. Ellicott refuses the inference outright: the word is the equivalent of lives, the vision telling that their lives had been sacrificed; it has been made a resting-place for an argument respecting the intermediate state, but there is no ground for this, it is quite beside the object of the seal.

On the cry, Henry works the ethics. Even the spirits of just men made perfect retain a proper resentment of the wrong they have sustained; and though they die in charity, praying as Christ did that God would forgive, they desire that for the honour of God and the gospel he take a just revenge upon the sin of persecution, even while he pardons and saves the persecutors — committing their cause to him to whom vengeance belongeth. Barnes reaches the same place by another road: they do not doubt that God will avenge but ask only how long, and it is not right to desire revenge, only that justice be done and the government of God vindicated. He adds that judge may mean either judge us, that is vindicate us, or judge them.

What the seal is for divides them again. Ellicott makes it a statement about the church: its mission can only be carried out in suffering, the martyrs laying down their lives at the altar’s foot as the victims’ blood was poured there, and Paul using the same imagery when he says he is ready to be poured out. Robertson dates it to the persecutions the readers knew, under Nero and again under Domitian, and reads the cause as loyalty to Christ against emperor-worship. Gill dates it two centuries later, to the times of Diocletian, a very dark time for both church and empire, where instead of a living creature’s voice John hears the voice of martyrs. Wesley keeps to his structure: the three latter seals all refer to the invisible world, the fifth to the happy dead, the sixth to the unhappy, the seventh to the angels. From the delay he draws a conclusion no one else draws: since their blood is to be avenged upon Babylon by and by but not yet, the plagues of the fourth seal do not concern Rome in particular.
10:
Who is actually crying is the question, and most of them answer that it is not the martyrs. Clarke says their blood, like Abel’s, cried for vengeance, and denies anything vindictive in those happy and holy souls who had shed it. Ellicott builds it out: by a dramatic figure the slain are shown crying for retribution, but it is not the Christians themselves who cry, any more than it was Abel himself who cried from the ground — it was the blood of Abel. The forgotten wrongs of generations come forth from oblivion and cry for vengeance; it is a poetical description, but not fiction: the laws of God avenge themselves, though the victims do not live to see it.

Gill takes the cry the other way, making a doctrine of its loudness. They cried with great ardour and fervency, being pressing and importunate, which shows they were awake and not asleep — that the soul does not sleep with the body in the grave, nor lie after death insensible, as some imagine. He reads the white robe the same way: a token of innocence, that they were not slain for any capital crime, and of the happiness which souls in a separate state, before the resurrection morn, partake.

The title they use draws the philologists. Robertson notes it is the correlative of servant, and here alone in this book applied to God; Wesley says it properly signifies the master of a family, beautifully used by those who are peculiarly of the household of God. Clarke expands each epithet: sovereign Lord, supreme Ruler, exercising unlimited and uncontrolled authority; holy in his own nature, hating iniquity; true in all his promises and threatenings. Robertson adds that the idiom returns later in the book and in the parable of the unjust judge, a passage which goes far to answer many questions in theodicy. Barnes has nothing here: his notes on both verses survive only as marginal cross-references, to Zechariah’s own how long, to the song of Moses, to the rewarding of the servants at the seventh trumpet, and to the word that they without us should not be made perfect.

On who is to be punished, Clarke stands alone. Those that dwell on the earth probably means the persecuting Jews, since they dwelt upon that land, a form of speech by which Judea is often signified; and the little season declares that when the cup of their iniquity should be full they should be punished in a mass. If the book was written before the destruction of Jerusalem, as is most likely, that season is the space between their martyrdom and the fall of the city under Vespasian and Titus.

Wesley measures the season rather than dating its end. Two classes of martyrs are specified, the former killed under heathen Rome and the latter under papal Rome, the former commanded to rest till the latter are added to them; and since a time in this book denotes 1111 years, this one ran from 98 to 1209, from Trajan’s persecution to the first crusade against the Waldenses. He is careful about what the promise does not say: it is not that immediately after this time vengeance shall be executed, but only that their brethren and fellowservants will come to them, this event preceding the other with some space between. Ellicott and Robertson read the rest more quietly. It does not mean they cease their cry, says Ellicott, for the saints have never cried for vengeance, but that they rest in joy and felicity while their fellow-sufferers achieve their work. Robertson allows both senses, rest from the cry and rest in peace, and notes what the promise implies: more persecution is coming. Ellicott finds one more sense in the robe: the excommunicated in one age are often the canonised of the next, for the dull world learns slowly and its purest honours are posthumous.
12:
Gill clears the ground first, and his survey is the fullest. Some refer this seal to the destruction of Jerusalem, on the likeness of the expressions; but that was past many years before the seal was opened, and though it was a day of the Lamb’s wrath upon that people, they had no sense of him nor apprehension of his wrath, imputing their calamity to their own quarrels. Others take it for the destruction of the Roman empire by Goths, Huns and Vandals; but the empire stood some hundreds of years after the fifth seal ended and this opened. His third objection is lost: the block breaks off mid-sentence at exactly two hundred words.

Barnes takes his usual road. All the symbols denote consternation and change, but each is significant and something must answer to each; and this is the seal that convinces him of the panorama, every item being paintable — the heaving ground, the trembling hills, the falling cities, the blackened sun, the moon turned to blood. He insists the earthquake is a figure: there are but three literal earthquakes in Scripture, the one before Elijah, the one in Uzziah’s days and the one at the Saviour’s death, all the rest emblematic of civil commotions. Standing alone it would denote great agitation, as if states and empires were tumbling to ruin, and the falling stars mean princes brought down from their thrones. Henry says it in one line: the foundations of churches and states would be terribly shaken.

Robertson gives the strongest caution against reading it flatly. The sackcloth is the coarse hair of the black goat, clinging like a sack, the garb of mourners and austere prophets; and the earthquake is no local one such as those common in Asia Minor. Then the argument: Peter took Joel’s sun turned into darkness and moon into blood as pointing to the day of Pentecost, and his reading of Joel should make us cautious about too literal an exegesis of these grand symbols.

Clarke and Gill read the seal as Constantine, and match it item for item. The earthquake is a most stupendous change in the civil and religious constitution of the world; the sun is the ancient pagan government of the empire, darkened; the moon is its ecclesiastical state, its rites abrogated and its temples turned into places for Christian worship; the stars are the gods and goddesses, demi-gods and deified heroes of the mythological heaven, prostrated indiscriminately; the heaven rolled up is the whole system of pagan worship shrivelled as a parchment scroll in a strong fire; the mountains are the props of the empire, its allies and tributary kings; the islands are the heathen temples with their precincts. Gill adds the history: the idol temples being opened, the images were exposed and found stuffed with hay and straw, which brought them into great contempt, and the idolatrous priests were discharged by Constantine.

Wesley stands outside all of it. This seal, he says, points out God’s judgment on the wicked departed: the end of the world was set before those unhappy spirits, a representation made without any of it being perceived upon earth. Where the others allegorise, he takes the astronomy literally — the stars fell towards the earth, yea, and so they surely will, let astronomers fix their magnitude as they please — and where they explain the scroll away, he finds a rule of style: when scripture compares a very great thing with a little, the majesty of God is highly exalted. His last remark is the smallest and best: what a mountain is to the land, that an island is to the sea. Barnes and Robertson end on the figs: winter figs that hang under the leaves and never ripen, falling easily in spring when a great wind shakes the tree — the point being the ease with which stars are shaken from their places.
15:
Barnes walks the list and gives each rank its reason: the rich, whose wealth would not secure them; the commanders of armies, who tremble like other men; the mighty, now powerless to withstand him. On bondman he stops. The word does not necessarily denote a slave, though the connexion demands it here, standing in contrast with freeman; but since this does not refer to the end of the world, the word determines nothing as to whether slavery is to continue on the earth. Robertson works the list philologically — the grandees are the persecuting proconsuls, the chief captains commanders of thousands — and adds the two whom terror least expects to reach: the complacent rich, and the strong, who usually scoff at fear.

Clarke reads every rank as Constantine’s defeated: the secular powers who had supported the pagan worship, the slaves addicted in life and limb to their owners, the freedmen attached by gratitude to their liberators — all astonished at the overthrow of the heathen empire. He quotes a rule of prophetic style: after describing a thing symbolically the prophets represent it again in plainer language, so the kings of the earth are Maximin, Galerius, Maxentius and Licinius, routed and dispersed. Gill supplies what became of them: they chose death rather than life — Diocletian, invited by Constantine to a marriage feast and then threatened by letters, poisoned himself, and others did the same.

On the cry to the rocks they converge. Barnes traces it to Hosea and to the Saviour’s use of it on the way to the cross, and reads it as the desire to be crushed by falling rocks rather than by an uplifted arm. Robertson notes the two imperatives come in inverted order from Hosea, in the tense of urgency — do it now — and puts the point best: what sinners dread most is not death but the revealed Presence of God. Wesley adds that the rocks were tottering already from the earthquake five verses back, and that these were rocks on high, besought to fall upon them.

The wrath of the Lamb troubles Barnes and delights Robertson. Barnes concedes the incongruity between wrath and Lamb, resolving it by making Lamb a proper name: he comes forth to execute wrath not as a Lamb but as the Son of God who bore that name. Robertson keeps the collision: the Lamb is the Lion again in the terribleness of his wrath. Gill notes the Latin and Syriac read of their wrath, of both him on the throne and of the Lamb, and takes it as the answer to the martyrs’ cry at the fifth seal. Clarke says they now saw these judgments came from the Almighty, and that Christ was destroying them for their persecutions of his followers.

The closing question gets two different answers. Robertson reports the view that the declaration the great day is come is the mistaken cry of men in terror at the portents bursting upon them, and grants something is to be said for it, since it denies that John commits himself to this being the end of the ages; the question is rhetorical, from the frightened crowds, and its only answer is the command to keep awake and pray for strength to stand. Ellicott takes it as the question of questions. The thought comes from Malachi: every advent of Christ is the advent of one whose fan is in his hand — the advent in the flesh, the advents in providence, the fall of Jerusalem, the overthrow of pagan Rome, and much more the closing advent. He reads the seal as deliberately incomplete: the world is stirred at the tread of the approaching Christ, then the vision melts away, and one asks what is left for the seventh to tell. His answer is the next chapter: they shall stand who are sealed with the seal of the living God.
